slides.title: Sector Exposure & Executive Risk Outlook
slides.decision: Treat Media & Cultural Services cyber risk as a shared-platform, live-output and revenue-continuity issue.
slides.executive_conclusion: Exposure is concentrated in shared front-of-house platforms and live-output integrity and reaches the financial system mainly through revenue lines, media-group credit and long recovery tails.
slides.visual_type: Judgement table with confidence and change conditions

elements.visible_text: Media & Cultural Services cyber exposure is concentrated in shared front-of-house platforms and live-output integrity; it reaches the financial system mainly through revenue lines, media-group credit and long recovery tails; ransom payments are rarely disclosed, so their role cannot be assessed.

Evidence base: public records for 1 September 2025 to 15 October 2026 across the EU, EEA and UK with global comparison - institution, ministry, prosecutor, regulator and court releases; company filings; ENISA, EEAS, Cloudflare and UK official statistics.

Footprint: 8.9 million people worked in EU cultural employment in 2025 (4.3% of jobs) and UK creative industries produced 5.5% of gross value added in 2024. Media drew 14.2% of mitigated DDoS requests on one large network in H1 2026, more than any other industry.
Shared ticketing, payment, cloud and content delivery platforms are the best-documented disruption pathway Medium Disclosed content or archive losses larger than access effects

slides.title: Key Threats & Top 5 Cyber Attacks
slides.decision: Weight reviews toward shared suppliers, live-output equipment and catalogue protection.
slides.executive_conclusion: Five incidents meet the evidence standard; shared platforms, signal paths and catalogues are exposure points alongside institutions' own networks.
slides.visual_type: Named incident table with pattern list

elements.visible_text: Five incidents meet the evidence standard; together with a shared ticketing outage known mainly from media relays, they show that signal paths, catalogues, customer data and shared platforms are exposure points alongside institutions' own networks.

Threat pathways (patterns, not attacks): P1 ransomware and extortion; P2 shared ticketing, payment and SaaS integrations; P3 broadcast signal and content insertion; P4 hacktivist DDoS and information manipulation around conflicts, elections and live events; P5 content theft; P6 personal-data exposure and litigation.
ENISA found broadcast media mostly faced hacktivist disruption of public-facing sites in 2025; the EEAS counted 540 manipulation incidents, including impersonation of established outlets.

slides.title: Financial Impact: Media & Cultural Services
slides.decision: Monitor revenue-line and credit signals rather than ransom or response-cost headlines.
slides.executive_conclusion: Public financial evidence is sparse and not additive; quantified losses come through curtailed revenue lines and slow recovery, and in one case became additional debt.

elements.visible_text: Public financial evidence is sparse and cannot be added up; where quantified, losses come through curtailed revenue lines and slow recovery, and in one case were converted into additional debt.

Evidence base: company filings from a US newspaper group and a Japanese publisher, British Library annual reports, institution notices and a court record; the two company attacks predate the period, their disclosures do not.

Transmission is conditional: advertising and subscription dips, ticketing outages with phishing follow-on, lender waivers, insurance recoveries that lag costs, and public funding that absorbs cultural-body losses.

slides.title: Financial Impact: Worst-Case Scenarios
slides.decision: Use three distinct stress pathways to test counterparty dependency mapping.
slides.executive_conclusion: Three distinct pathways converge on lost revenue channels and long recovery; they are stress narratives, not forecasts.

elements.visible_text: Three distinct stress pathways - a shared platform failure, a targeted hit on a broadcaster or national institution, and a compromised shared supplier - converge on lost revenue channels, with recovery ranging from hours to years; they are stress narratives, not forecasts or loss estimates.

elements.visible_text: Evidence: a 14.5-hour cloud regional disruption and a 6-hour delivery-network outage in late 2025; Dresden, US newspaper and British Library recovery records; one ticketing provider serving France's national monuments network.
Interpretation: scenario 1 is broad and short, scenario 2 narrow and deep, scenario 3 broad and deep through one supplier.
Management implication: ask which major counterparties share the same delivery, ticketing and playout suppliers, and whether rights-sensitive live events have tested fallback.
Limitation: no probabilities are assigned because no defensible external basis exists; durations are illustrative and no 2026 cloud or delivery-network outage of comparable scale was found.

slides.title: Case Study: Dresden State Art Collections Cyberattack
slides.decision: Treat online-sales and card-payment loss at public cultural counterparties as a foreseeable multi-week event.
slides.executive_conclusion: The security system kept running and museums stayed open while revenue channels recovered last.

elements.visible_text: A deliberate attack on Saxony's state museum network removed the online shop, visitor services and card payment while the security system kept running and museums stayed open; information channels returned within days and revenue channels recovered last.

Evidence base: institution and ministry releases of 22 and 29 January 2026, a prosecutor and state police release of 19 February 2026 and a ministerial answer relayed in July 2026; selected as the recent EU case with the most complete primary chronology.
Interpretation: activity over several days before containment points to detection lag; information channels returned within a week, transactional channels within about a month (media-reported).
Intrusion 17-21 January Attack activity over several days, per a ministerial answer

row_cells: Shop and visitor services offline; security system unaffected; museums open

slides.title: Systemic Dependencies & Regulatory Outlook
slides.decision: Assess supplier regulation status, AI-content controls and product reporting in counterparty reviews.
slides.executive_conclusion: The sector sits outside horizontal cyber regimes; resilience depends on regulated providers and media and product rules.
slides.visual_type: Dependency chain text and regime status table

elements.visible_text: Media and culture are not a named sector under NIS2, the CER Directive or the UK NIS Regulations, so resilience depends on regulated providers, product rules and media-specific law, while shared ticketing, cloud and signal paths concentrate risk that no regime addresses through the sector itself.

Evidenced dependency chains: shared ticketing -> national monuments network; cloud region -> streaming and online games; delivery network -> news and ticketing sites; streaming encoders and satellite uplinks -> live output.
Interpretation: in-period movement came from AI transparency, product reporting and a US broadcast rule, not from horizontal cyber law; the UK bill is not yet law.

slides.title: Mitigation Strategies & Security Framework
slides.decision: Assign each priority a 1LoD owner, completion artefact and escalation trigger.
slides.executive_conclusion: Six evidence-linked priorities address the pathways without asserting any institution's control gaps.

elements.visible_text: Six evidence-linked priorities address the pathways: map shared front-of-house suppliers, harden live-output equipment, segregate and test recovery, contain payment fraud after data exposure, protect brand provenance, and align credit and funding with long recovery.
A1 Shared platforms (0-6 months) Which ticketing, payment, cloud and delivery providers do top counterparties share? Dependency map; fallback tests Supplier incident or prosecutor notice
row_cells: Which ticketing, payment, cloud and delivery providers do top counterparties share?

elements.visible_text: A2 Live-output integrity (0-6 months) Do broadcasters meet a password, patch and segmentation baseline for content insertion? Baseline attestation Regulator device warning; hijack report
row_cells: Do broadcasters meet a password, patch and segmentation baseline for content insertion?

elements.visible_text: A3 Segregation and recovery (3-12 months) Are security, building and playout systems separate from corporate IT? Segregation and restoration tests Sector incident notice
row_cells: Are security, building and playout systems separate from corporate IT?

elements.visible_text: A4 Payment fraud (0-3 months) Are fraud typologies monitored after ticket-holder data exposure? Monitoring and verification procedure Ticketing or subscriber data notice
row_cells: Are fraud typologies monitored after ticket-holder data exposure?

elements.visible_text: A5 Provenance (6-12 months) How are brand impersonation and AI-generated content detected and labelled? Provenance and labelling procedure Manipulation alert; election calendar
row_cells: How are brand impersonation and AI-generated content detected and labelled?

elements.visible_text: A6 Credit and funding (6-12 months) What recovery time, insurance and waiver triggers apply to media borrowers? Recovery objectives; insurance schedule Waiver or amendment request
row_cells: What recovery time, insurance and waiver triggers apply to media borrowers?

elements.visible_text: Evidence base: the US alerting order, Dresden and British Library recovery records, ticketing data exposure, EEAS impersonation findings, lender waivers at a US newspaper group and UK charity insurance coverage.
Frameworks are reference vocabularies, not law: NIST CSF 2.0, ISO/IEC 27001 and 27036, EBU R 148, C2PA content provenance and PCI DSS v4.0.1.
Management implication: give each priority a 1LoD owner and a dated completion artefact, and escalate to the Risk Committee when a monitoring trigger fires.
Limitation: actions are sector priorities drawn from public evidence, not findings about any institution's controls, losses or risk appetite.
